lessons.title: Structure and bonding of carbon
lessons.summary: Explore the different forms of carbon (diamond, graphite, graphene, fullerenes and nanotubes) and explain how each one's structure and bonding give it its properties and uses.
objectives: I can describe the structure of diamond and explain its hardness and high melting point.
I can describe the structure of graphite and explain why it is soft and conducts electricity.
I can describe graphene and fullerenes, including buckminsterfullerene and carbon nanotubes.
I can link the properties of each form of carbon to its uses.

activities.title: One element, many structures
activities.content:
## Why carbon is special

A carbon atom has **four outer electrons**, so it can form **four covalent bonds**. Because carbon atoms bond so readily with each other, the same element can be arranged into completely different structures with completely different properties. The pencil lead you write with and the diamond in a ring are both pure carbon.

In this lesson you will meet five arrangements:

| Form | Shape of structure | Bonds per carbon |
|---|---|---|
| Diamond | 3D giant lattice | 4 |
| Graphite | flat layers of hexagons | 3 |
| Graphene | a single layer of graphite | 3 |
| Fullerenes | hollow balls or tubes | 3 |

The number of bonds each carbon makes is the key to everything. Four bonds leave no spare electrons; three bonds leave one electron per atom **delocalised**, free to move and conduct electricity. Keep asking "three or four bonds?" and the properties will follow.

activities.title: Diamond
activities.content:
## Diamond

In diamond, every carbon atom is joined to **four other carbon atoms** by strong covalent bonds. The bonds point towards the corners of a tetrahedron, and the pattern repeats in every direction to give a rigid **giant covalent structure**.

Properties and their explanations:

- **Very hard.** Every atom is locked into the network by four strong bonds, so there are no weak points and the layers cannot move. Diamond is the hardest natural substance, which is why it is used on the tips of drill bits and cutting tools.
- **Very high melting point** (around 3550 °C). Melting means breaking many strong covalent bonds, which needs an enormous amount of energy.
- **Does not conduct electricity.** All four outer electrons on each atom are used in bonding, so there are **no delocalised electrons** to carry charge.

In an exam, "strong covalent bonds" on its own is not enough for the hardness mark. You need the idea that each atom has **four** bonds in a **rigid 3D network**.

question.text: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
question.hint: How many of carbon's four outer electrons are used up in bonding?
question.explanation: Each carbon in diamond uses all four outer electrons to form covalent bonds, so there are no delocalised electrons free to carry charge.

options.text: All the outer electrons are used in covalent bonds, so none are free to move
The covalent bonds are too weak to carry current
options.feedback: The bonds are strong; strength is not what decides conductivity.

options.text: It is made of ions that cannot move

activities.title: Graphite
activities.content:
## Graphite

In graphite, each carbon atom forms **three covalent bonds** to other carbon atoms, producing flat sheets of **hexagonal rings**. The sheets stack on top of each other in **layers**, and there are **no covalent bonds between the layers**, only weak forces.

That structure explains three properties:

- **Soft and slippery.** The layers can **slide over each other** because only weak forces hold them together. This is why graphite is used as pencil "lead" (layers rub off onto paper) and as a dry **lubricant**.
- **High melting point.** Within each layer the covalent bonds are strong, and many must be broken to melt it, so graphite still has a very high melting point despite being soft.
- **Conducts electricity and heat.** Each carbon uses only three of its four outer electrons for bonding. The fourth is **delocalised** and can move along the layers, carrying charge. Graphite is used for **electrodes**, for example in electrolysis.

Graphite is a rare thing: a non-metal that conducts electricity. In that one way it behaves like a metal, and for the same reason, delocalised electrons.

activities.title: Worked example: comparing diamond and graphite
activities.content:
**Explain why diamond is used for cutting tools but graphite is used as a lubricant, even though both are pure carbon.**

*Diamond:* each atom has **four** strong covalent bonds in a rigid **3D** network. No part of the structure can move relative to another, so it is extremely hard and can cut other materials.

*Graphite:* each atom has only **three** covalent bonds, giving flat **layers**. There are **no covalent bonds between layers**, just weak forces, so the layers **slide** easily. A thin film of graphite lets surfaces glide over each other, which is what a lubricant needs.

The two structures share strong covalent bonds and high melting points; they differ in how many bonds each atom makes and, therefore, whether layers exist.

question.text: Explain why graphite can conduct electricity.
question.hint: Count the bonds on each carbon atom and think about what happens to the spare electron.
question.explanation: Each carbon atom in graphite forms only three covalent bonds, so one outer electron per atom is delocalised. These delocalised electrons are free to move through the layers and carry electrical charge.

markScheme.criterion: Each carbon forms only three bonds / one electron per atom is not used in bonding
Delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge

activities.title: Graphene
activities.content:
## Graphene

**Graphene** is a **single layer of graphite**: a sheet of carbon atoms just **one atom thick**, arranged in hexagons, with each atom bonded to three others. It was first isolated in 2004 by peeling layers from graphite with sticky tape, and it turned out to have remarkable properties.

- **Extremely strong.** The covalent bonds within the sheet are strong and there are no weak spots, so graphene is one of the strongest materials ever tested, yet it is so thin that it is almost transparent.
- **Conducts electricity.** Like graphite, each atom has one delocalised electron, and with only one layer these electrons move very freely.
- **Flexible and light.** A single atomic layer can bend without breaking.

Possible uses include **flexible touch screens**, **composites** that add strength without much weight, faster **electronic components** and **filters** and sensors. Graphene is still expensive to make in large, flawless sheets, so many of these uses are at the research stage.

Remember the definition: graphene is *one* layer; graphite is *many* stacked layers.

question.text: True or false: graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, one atom thick, in which each carbon atom is bonded to three others.
question.hint: Picture graphite and imagine lifting off one sheet.
question.explanation: True. Graphene is exactly one layer of graphite: a hexagonal sheet of carbon atoms each bonded to three neighbours.

activities.title: Fullerenes and nanotubes
activities.content:
## Fullerenes

**Fullerenes** are molecules of carbon atoms with **hollow shapes**. The carbon atoms are arranged in hexagonal rings, often with some five- or seven-membered rings too, which let a flat sheet curve into a ball or tube.

**Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀**, was the first fullerene discovered. It is a **hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms**, like a tiny football, and it exists as separate molecules, so it is a simple molecular substance with a fairly low melting point compared with diamond. Fullerene molecules can be used to **deliver drugs** inside the body (a medicine trapped inside the cage), as **lubricants** (the balls roll over each other) and as **catalysts**, because their large surface area gives plenty of room for reactions.

**Carbon nanotubes** are **cylindrical fullerenes**: a graphene sheet rolled into a tube with a very high **length-to-diameter ratio**. Their properties:

- **Very high tensile strength** (hard to snap when pulled), so they **reinforce** materials such as tennis rackets and sports equipment.
- **Conduct electricity and heat**, useful in nanotechnology and **electronics**.

Think of the family tree: graphene is a flat sheet; roll it into a tube for a nanotube; wrap it into a ball for C₆₀.

activities.title: Worked example: choosing a form of carbon
activities.content:
**A company wants a material to strengthen a lightweight bicycle frame. Which form of carbon should it choose, and why?**

*Choice:* **carbon nanotubes**, mixed into the frame material as a composite.

*Why:* nanotubes have a **very high tensile strength** because of the strong covalent bonds running along the tube, and they are extremely **light** because they are hollow and made of carbon. A small amount added to a resin adds a lot of strength without much extra mass.

*Why not the others?* Diamond is hard but brittle and cannot be woven into a frame. Graphite is soft because its layers slide, so it adds no strength. C₆₀ is a lubricant and drug carrier, not a reinforcing fibre.

In a "choose and justify" question, always give a property **and** link it to the job.

question.text: Match each form of carbon to a typical use.
question.hint: Think about which property each use needs: hardness, sliding layers, hollow cages or high tensile strength.
question.explanation: Diamond is hard so is used for cutting tools; graphite's sliding layers make it a lubricant; C₆₀ cages can carry drugs; nanotubes have high tensile strength so they reinforce materials.

question.text: How many carbon atoms are there in one molecule of buckminsterfullerene?
question.hint: The number is in its formula.
question.explanation: Buckminsterfullerene has the formula C₆₀, so each molecule contains 60 carbon atoms.

question.text:
Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon atoms.

(a) Explain why diamond is very hard. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why graphite is soft. (2 marks)

(c) State one property that diamond and graphite have in common and explain it. (1 mark)
question.hint: Compare the number of bonds per atom and whether the structure has layers. For (c), think about melting point.
question.explanation: (a) Each carbon atom forms four strong covalent bonds in a rigid three-dimensional giant structure, so atoms cannot move past each other. (b) Each carbon atom forms only three bonds, giving layers with no covalent bonds between them, only weak forces, so the layers slide over each other. (c) Both have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt them.

markScheme.criterion: Each carbon atom in diamond forms four strong covalent bonds
In a rigid 3D giant covalent structure / lattice with no layers to move
Graphite: each carbon forms three bonds, giving layers
No covalent bonds between layers / weak forces between layers so layers can slide
Both have high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Carbon forms **four covalent bonds**, so it can build several very different structures.
- **Diamond**: 4 bonds per atom, rigid 3D lattice; very hard, very high melting point, no conduction.
- **Graphite**: 3 bonds per atom, layers of hexagons; soft (layers slide), high melting point, **conducts** because of delocalised electrons.
- **Graphene**: one layer of graphite; extremely strong, conducts, used in electronics and composites.
- **Fullerenes**: hollow cages (C₆₀) or **nanotubes**; used for drug delivery, lubricants, catalysts and reinforcing materials.
- Ask "three bonds or four?" to predict whether a form of carbon conducts.

practiceQuestions.text: How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in diamond?
practiceQuestions.hint: Carbon has four outer electrons and uses them all in diamond.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Each carbon atom in diamond is bonded to four others.

options.feedback: Three is the number in graphite and graphene.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: graphite has a low melting point because its layers are held together by weak forces.
practiceQuestions.hint: Melting graphite means breaking the bonds within the layers, not just separating the layers.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Although the forces between layers are weak, melting requires breaking the many strong covalent bonds within the layers, so graphite has a very high melting point.

metadata.blanksText: Graphene is a single ___ of graphite, one atom thick. A carbon nanotube is a sheet of graphene rolled into a ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: Think of a sheet of paper and what you can roll it into.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Graphene is a single layer; rolling it gives a cylinder (tube).

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following forms of carbon conduct electricity? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Conduction needs delocalised electrons, which come from atoms with only three bonds.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Graphite and graphene both have one delocalised electron per atom, so they conduct. Diamond does not, because all four electrons are used in bonding.

practiceQuestions.text: A carbon nanotube has a diameter of 2 nm and a length of 4000 nm. Calculate its length-to-diameter ratio.
practiceQuestions.hint: Divide the length by the diameter.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 4000 ÷ 2 = 2000. Nanotubes have very high length-to-diameter ratios, which contributes to their usefulness as reinforcing fibres.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these steps in order to describe how the structure of graphite explains its use as a lubricant.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start with the bonding and end with the use.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Three bonds per atom create layers; weak forces between the layers let them slide; sliding layers reduce friction, which is what a lubricant does.
order: Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds, making flat layers
Only weak forces exist between the layers
The layers can slide over each other easily
Surfaces coated in graphite move past each other with less friction

practiceQuestions.text: Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, has a much lower melting point than diamond. Explain why.
practiceQuestions.hint: Is C₆₀ a giant structure or made of separate molecules?
practiceQuestions.explanation: C₆₀ is made of separate molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces, which need little energy to overcome. Diamond is a giant covalent structure where strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it.

markScheme.criterion: C60 consists of separate / simple molecules
Only weak intermolecular forces between molecules need to be overcome (whereas diamond needs strong covalent bonds broken)

practiceQuestions.text: Which property of carbon nanotubes makes them suitable for strengthening a tennis racket?
practiceQuestions.hint: A reinforcing fibre must resist being pulled apart.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Nanotubes have very high tensile strength thanks to strong covalent bonds along the tube, so they resist stretching and snapping.

options.feedback: That is a use of spherical fullerenes such as C₆₀.

practiceQuestions.text:
Graphene is being tested for use in flexible touch screens.

(a) Describe the structure of graphene. (2 marks)

(b) Explain two properties of graphene that make it suitable for a flexible touch screen. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a): thickness and number of bonds per atom. For (b): a touch screen must carry current and bend.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, one atom thick, arranged in hexagons with each atom covalently bonded to three others. (b) It conducts electricity because each atom has a delocalised electron; it is thin and flexible so it bends without breaking, and it is strong and nearly transparent.

markScheme.criterion: A single layer of carbon atoms / one atom thick
Each carbon bonded to three others in hexagons
Conducts electricity because of delocalised electrons
Flexible / thin / strong / transparent

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following best describes a fullerene?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think of the shape of C₆₀.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes, such as spheres or tubes, based on hexagonal rings.

options.text: A molecule of carbon atoms arranged in a hollow shape such as a sphere or tube
A giant covalent structure of carbon atoms in a 3D lattice
A single flat sheet of carbon atoms
A mixture of carbon and hydrogen atoms

practiceQuestions.text: Which statement explains why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not?
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare how many of the four outer electrons each carbon atom uses for bonding in the two structures.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In graphite each carbon atom bonds to only three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom to carry charge. In diamond every carbon uses all four outer electrons in covalent bonds, so no electrons are free to move.

options.text: Each carbon in graphite has one delocalised electron, but in diamond all four outer electrons are used in bonds
Graphite contains metal ions and diamond does not
options.feedback: Both are made only of carbon atoms.

options.text: The covalent bonds in graphite are weaker, so electrons escape from them
options.feedback: The bonds within a graphite layer are as strong as those in diamond; bond strength does not decide conductivity.

options.text: Diamond has fewer electrons per atom than graphite

practiceQuestions.text: Graphene is being used to make very thin electrical wires. Explain why graphene conducts electricity.
practiceQuestions.hint: How many bonds does each carbon atom in graphene form, and what happens to its remaining outer electron?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Each carbon atom in graphene forms only three covalent bonds, so one outer electron per atom is not used in bonding. These electrons are delocalised across the sheet and are free to move, so they can carry electrical charge.

markScheme.criterion: Each carbon forms only three bonds / one electron per atom is not used in bonding
Delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a carbon nanotube can be thought of as a single sheet of graphene rolled up into a hollow cylinder.
practiceQuestions.hint: Picture a sheet of hexagons and imagine curling it round until the edges meet.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. A carbon nanotube is a cylindrical fullerene: a layer of hexagonally bonded carbon atoms, like graphene, rolled into a tube with a hollow centre.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each form of carbon to a use that depends on its properties.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about which form is transparent and flexible, which is hardest, which conducts and stands up to heat, and which makes tiny conducting tubes.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Graphene is a transparent, flexible conductor, ideal for touch screens. Diamond's hardness makes it suitable for cutting glass. Graphite conducts and has a very high melting point, so it is used for electrodes. Carbon nanotubes conduct and are tiny, so they can act as wires in miniature circuits.

pairs.right: Transparent conducting layer in a flexible touch screen
Tiny wires in miniature electronic circuits

practiceQuestions.text: In a molecule of buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, how many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom bonded to?
practiceQuestions.hint: The carbon atoms in fullerenes are arranged in hexagonal rings, like the atoms in a layer of graphite.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Each carbon atom in C₆₀ is bonded to three other carbon atoms, the same as in graphite and graphene.

practiceQuestions.text:
Diamond and graphite are both giant covalent structures made of carbon atoms.

(a) Explain why diamond has a very high melting point. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. (2 marks)

(c) State one use of graphite that depends on its layered structure and explain why the layers make it suitable. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), count the bonds per atom and think about the energy needed to break them. For (b), consider what happens to the fourth outer electron in each structure. For (c), think about pencils or lubricants.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Each carbon atom in diamond forms four strong covalent bonds, and a very large amount of energy is needed to break these many strong bonds. (b) In graphite each carbon forms only three bonds, so one electron per atom is delocalised and free to carry charge; in diamond all four outer electrons are used in bonding, so there are no free electrons. (c) Graphite is used as a lubricant (or in pencils) because there are only weak forces between the layers, so the layers slide over each other easily.

markScheme.criterion: Each carbon atom in diamond forms four strong covalent bonds
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken, needing a lot of energy
Graphite: each carbon forms three bonds, so one electron per atom is delocalised
Diamond: all four outer electrons are used in bonding, so no electrons are free to move
Lubricant / pencil because weak forces between layers let them slide
